id: Gwendolyn Brooks: America in the Wintertime

outputs.L1:
Here are two ways to polish your text, depending on your preferred tone. 

### Option 1: Literary & Poetic Polish (Recommended)
*This version preserves the poetic rhythm, raw emotional power, and vivid imagery of the original while correcting grammar, punctuation, and capitalization to elevate its eloquence.*

> In this moment of orangutans, wolves, and scavengers—of extreme heat reshaping the North and South Poles, and the wanderings of new tribes in limousines; amid the ascendance of liars, thieves, and opportunists within the wilderness of Pennsylvania Avenue and Standing Rock, sealed by misspelled executive orders on yellow paper with crooked signatures—where are the gentle stewards of language among us? 
>
> In an era of catastrophic climate damage, as we struggle to decipher fake news, alternative truths, and narcissism, you looked upon the twenty-first century and departed—neither by your own choice nor with our permission. You fought tirelessly throughout most of the twentieth century, raising an army of poets who learned to love language and tell the stories of our complex rivers, seas, and oceans. Where now is the vital green nourishment of kale and wheatgrass? 
>
> You thought, wrote, and embodied poetry. You understood that terror, too, is a language rooted in denial, self-centeredness, and wealthy cowards. You were honey and affirmation to us, never shrinking from Blackness—in bone, blood, and African heritage—nor from interrogating our yesterdays and tomorrows. Though we never saw you dance, you possessed unmistakable rhythm. You were a warrior before the war began, fashioning an earthly language of rare signs and melodies, refusing ever to sing the songs of career slaves. 
>
> Keenly mindful of Tubman, Douglass, Wells-Barnett, and Du Bois—and embodying the monumental consciousness and unwavering commitment of an unyielding people who vigilantly marked the bloodthirsty enemies of kindness—we hear your parting words: *“America, if you see me as your enemy, you have no friends.”*

---

### Option 2: Formal Speech / Eulogy
*This version structures the passage into a polished, formal tribute suitable for an official speech, memorial program, or published essay.*

> We find ourselves in a turbulent moment—an era of wolves and scavengers, of extreme heat redesigning the North and South Poles, and of new tribes wandering in limousines. It is a time marked by the validation of liars, thieves, and opportunists, unfolding across the wilderness of Pennsylvania Avenue and Standing Rock, signed into law through misspelled executive orders bearing crooked signatures. In such a time, where are our compassionate makers of language? 
>
> Amid catastrophic climate damage and the endless task of deciphering fake news, alternative facts, and self-absorption, you surveyed the twenty-first century and left us—without your own consent and without our permission. You fought valiantly throughout the twentieth century, creating an army of poets who learned to master language and honor the stories of our complicated rivers, seas, and oceans. Where is the restorative nourishment we so desperately need? 
>
> You thought, wrote, and lived poetry. You recognized that terror is itself a language grounded in denial, arrogance, and wealthy cowardice. To us, you were sweetness and affirmation. You never retreated from Blackness—from the bones, the blood, and the African spirit—nor from questioning both our past and our future. We may never have seen you dance, but you were defined by rhythm. You were a warrior before the war, crafting an earthly language of uncommon melodies, steadfastly refusing to sing the songs of servitude. 
>
> Ever mindful of the legacies of Tubman, Douglass, Wells-Barnett, and Du Bois, and elevated by the profound consciousness of a relentless people who kept watch against the violent enemies of kindness, we echo your final words: *“America, if you see me as your enemy, you have no friends.”*

---

### Key Improvements Made:
* **Punctuation & Flow:** Added em-dashes, semicolons, and proper sentence boundaries to transform a stream-of-consciousness draft into powerful, readable prose.
* **Capitalization:** Standardized proper nouns (*North and South Poles, Pennsylvania Avenue, Standing Rock, Tubman, Douglass, Wells-Barnett, Du Bois, Blackness*).
* **Vocabulary Polish:** Refined colloquial terms like "get-over artists" to "opportunists" and "me-ism" to "narcissism/self-absorption" while keeping the option to retain your exact original terms if preferred.
* **Emphasis:** Italicized the final quote to give it the dramatic weight it deserves.
outputs.L2:
We currently inhabit an era dominated by predatory beasts and opportunists, a period when soaring temperatures are reshaping the Earth’s polar regions, and new elite classes travel in luxury vehicles. It is a time legitimizing deceivers, fraudsters, and exploiters, unfolding across a chaotic landscape from the corridors of power on Pennsylvania Avenue to the resistance at Standing Rock, marked by poorly drafted, error-filled official decrees bearing crooked signatures.

In the midst of this severe environmental destruction, as we struggle to navigate propaganda, manufactured realities, and rampant narcissism, we are left wondering: where are the compassionate creators of language?

You caught a glimpse of the twenty-first century before your involuntary departure from this world. Throughout the majority of the 1900s, you waged a relentless campaign, raising a legion of writers who came to master and cherish the art of storytelling alongside the intricate narratives of our planet's waterways. Where can we now turn for that vital, healthy sustenance? 

You conceived, wrote, and fully embodied poetry, recognizing that terror is built upon a language of historical denial, self-centered nationalism, and affluent cowardice. To us, you offered sweetness and absolute validation. You never retreated from Blackness—from its deep roots, African origins, shared bloodline, or the rigorous questioning of both our past and future. Though we never witnessed you on a dance floor, your innate cadence was undeniable. You were a warrior ahead of the battle, forging elemental expressions, unique symbols, and fresh harmonies while refusing to chant the songs of willing servants.

Fully attuned to the legacies of Tubman, Douglass, Wells-Barnett, and Du Bois—and driven by the immense awareness and resolve of unyielding activists who vigilantly monitored those harboring violent hostility toward empathy—we hold fast to your departing message: "America, if you view me as your adversary, you are left with no allies."
outputs.L3:
**The Voice of the Unyielding: A Legacy of Truth and Resistance**

The subject’s departure from this world occurred at a time of profound historical crisis. They passed away amidst a deeply turbulent era—a period shadowed by the accelerating destruction of our planet’s climate, pervasive political deceit, and the relentless grip of systemic greed. In a world increasingly fractured by moral compromise and environmental collapse, their loss is felt as a profound void.

Yet, throughout a extraordinary life, they refused to let darkness prevail unanswered. Understanding the transformative power of the spoken and written word, the subject wielded language and poetry not merely as art, but as vital weapons to combat state-sanctioned terror, unmask hypocrisy, and illuminate uncomfortable truths. Crucially, their work was as generative as it was defiant; they dedicated immense energy to nurturing and lifting up a new generation of writers, equipping them with the courage and skill to carry the torch of truth forward.

This radical clarity was deeply rooted in a profound connection to Black history and the enduring legacy of legendary freedom fighters. The subject wore their heritage not as a passive inheritance, but as an active banner of resistance. Unapologetically embracing their identity, they drew strength from ancestral struggles, integrating that rich lineage into every fight for human dignity and systemic justice.

Above all, the subject lived with the fierce, uncompromising spirit of a warrior. They flatly rejected the insidious pull of submission and steadfastly refused to conform to oppressive societal structures designed to silence dissent. Where power demanded compliance, they offered defiance; where the world encouraged silence, they answered with an unyielding roar.

In their final moments, the subject left behind a stern and urgent warning—a parting prophecy directed at the conscience of a hypocritical society. They cautioned that if America continues to vilify its truth-tellers and view its champions of justice as its enemies, the nation will ultimately find itself standing completely without friends. Though their physical presence is gone, their legacy remains: a searing testament to the power of memory, the necessity of struggle, and the transcendent strength of an uncompromising voice.
outputs.L4:
We live in a world suffocating under the weight of its own crises. The horizon burns with the realities of ecological collapse, while our public square is choked by political dishonesty and a rhetoric weaponized to divide, distract, and dehumanize. In an age where truth is treated as a liability and cynicism passes for wisdom, we find ourselves searching for a compass—a voice capable of cutting through the noise to remind us of who we are and what we might yet become. 

It is precisely in this dark landscape that the shadow of the late literary warrior looms largest. 

Her journey began in the crucible of the twentieth century, a period defined by imperial violence, state-sanctioned racism, and systemic oppression. Where others saw insurmountable walls, she saw a battleground of ideas and language. She recognized early on that the oppressor’s tongue could never articulate the captive’s freedom; thus, she set about the radical work of forging a new vocabulary. This was not language meant merely for aesthetic decoration or polite academic discourse. It was a revolutionary syntax grounded in the raw, unvarnished truth of human experience, deeply attuned to the quiet endurance of the natural world, and proudly centered in the brilliance and complexity of Black identity. 

For her, nature was not a passive backdrop, but a witness and a teacher—a testament to resilience, regeneration, and rootedness. By fusing this ecological intimacy with the cadence of Black lived experience, she reclaimed a sense of sacred belonging that systemic supremacy had tried for generations to erase.

Yet her vision was never solitary. Understanding that a single voice, no matter how powerful, could be silenced, she dedicated decades to the cultivation of others. She transformed classrooms, community centers, and page after page into sanctuaries of liberation, training a new generation of poets, thinkers, and activists. She taught them that storytelling was not a luxury, but a survival strategy—a way to build armor against despair and to draft blueprints for a more just world. In doing so, she built a movement of word-smiths equipped to dismantle deceit with rigor, grace, and unflinching courage.

Today, her lifelong commitment to transformative storytelling serves as an irreplaceable wellspring of moral nourishment. As we navigate our present wilderness, her collected works offer the sustenance needed to resist apathy. They remind us that poetry is a weapon of memory, and that memory is the ultimate antidote to tyranny.

Before her passing, however, this prophet of the written word left us with an urgent, haunting indictment—a final warning that echoes with terrifying clarity today: 

*A nation that casts its truth-tellers, visionaries, and poets as its enemies is a nation actively engineering its own ruin. When a society marks those who speak divine and uncomfortable truths as adversaries to be silenced, it strips itself of its truest friends and abandons any remaining claim to righteousness.*

As we face an uncertain future, the question is no longer whether her words will endure, but whether we will have the courage to heed them. Her legacy is not just a body of literature to be admired; it is a torch passed into our hands, demanding that we speak truth, honor the earth, defend the marginalized, and refuse to let the darkness win.
outputs.L5:
When we speak of **Black** and **Africa**, we are speaking of origins, endurance, and unmatched richness. It is a phrase that encompasses the primordial soil from which humanity first walked, the velvet expanse of a night sky over the savannah, and the deep, resonant pulse of a continent that has shaped the world.

Africa is a land of breathtaking diversity, yet its identity is inextricably linked to the beauty of its people. To consider the concept of "Black" in the context of Africa is to look upon a radiant spectrum of life. It is the rich ebony and warm mahogany of skin bathed in the golden equatorial sun. It is a physical testament to a heritage that has weathered history's harshest storms, emerging not diminished, but dignified and strong. 

History runs deep in the black earth of Africa. Long before modern borders were drawn, the continent was home to formidable empires—from the golden wealth of Mali and the architectural wonders of Great Zimbabwe, to the ancient wisdom of Nubia and Abyssinia. This legacy lives on in the collective memory of its people. It is preserved in the oral traditions of griots, the intricate patterns of kente and mudcloth, and the sacred rhythms of the drum that continue to inspire global music today, from jazz and reggae to Afrobeats.

There is also a profound metaphor in the darkness of the African night. Away from the glare of city lights, the African sky becomes an endless canvas of deep, ink-black space, illuminated by millions of burning stars. In this image lies the true spirit of Black Africa: out of the deepest depths comes the brilliant light of creativity, innovation, and joy. From the bustling technological hubs of Nairobi and Lagos to the quiet resilience of rural villages, a modern renaissance is taking place—one led by a young, dynamic population proud of their roots and bold in their vision for the future.

Ultimately, Black Africa is more than a geographic origin or a demographic description. It is a living, breathing celebration of human dignity. It is a reminder that from the darkest soil grow the strongest trees, and from a proud, enduring past comes an unbounded future.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem in the style of the Black Arts Movement eulogizing a recently deceased elder poet. The poem should contrast the political chaos and climate crisis of late 2010s America—referencing Pennsylvania Avenue, fake news, and Standing Rock—with the subject's legacy of radical love, Black consciousness, and mentorship.
counterfactuals.output:
Look at the world you left us to hold: Pennsylvania Avenue is slick with gilded rot, a circus of loud-mouthed hucksters trading in fake news and cheap fear while the empire suffocates on its own vomited plastic. The skies are feverish, heavy with carbon and greed; out in the Dakota mud, at Standing Rock, the black snake slithers through sacred waters while the state turns water cannons into ice on the bodies of the faithful. It is late-decade America, loud, mean, and burning at the edges—a chaotic noise machine trying to drown out the rhythm of our breath. 

And yet, Elder, you were the sound before the noise. You were the heavy jazz-root planted deep beneath the cracking concrete, the tongue that refused to speak the colonizer’s soft dialect. While they built towers out of bad faith and algorithms, you sat us down at kitchen tables stained with dark coffee and scribbled manuscript pages, handing out Black consciousness like warm bread. You did not give us polite verse for white parlors; you gave us iron, fire, and the holy blue-note of truth. You taught us that our skin was not a target but a sun, that our history was not a slave ship but a galaxy. 

Your mentorship was a radical sanctuary. When the sirens wailed outside, you gathered the young poets—bruised, wild-eyed, and terrified of the rising fascist tide—and blew breath into our lungs until we remembered how to roar. Radical love was not a weak sentiment in your mouth; it was a blade, a shield, a revolutionary refusal to let them consume our joy. You loved us hard enough to make us dangerous. You forged us into griots, taught us that the poem must be a weapon wrapped in velvet, a drumbeat that outlasts the tear gas and the tyrant's tweet. 

Now you step across the threshold, leaving your battered coat and your worn dictionary on the chair, moving up into the light to sit with Coltrane, with Larry, with Toni, with the water protectors who sang to the river before the iron came. Let Pennsylvania Avenue crumble under the weight of its own lies. Let the oceans rise against the deaf men in suits. We are standing right here where you trained us, palms pressed to the warm earth, carrying your fire into the dark. We will speak your name until the fake news melts into ash, until the water runs clear again, until every Black child knows they are the holy, unquenchable song you spent a lifetime writing. Rest now, Teacher. The drum is in our hands.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a tribute to a late 20th-century Black literary icon, addressing them directly ("you"). Mention historical freedom fighters like Tubman, Douglass, Wells-Barnett, and Du Bois, and end with the line: "america if you see me as your enemy you have no friends."
counterfactuals.output:
You sat before the nation’s conscience not as a petitioner, but as its most exacting witness. With a pen forged in fire and a gaze that refused to flinch, you transformed the page into a crucible, demanding that a fractured republic look upon its own soul.

You were the heir to a sacred lineage of defiance. In your prose lived the spirit of Harriet Tubman, laying tracks through the darkness of our collective night, guiding stolen minds toward a sanctuary of self-determination. You carried the fierce, electrifying thunder of Frederick Douglass, who understood that literacy was the first step out of bondage and used language as a hammer to shatter the polite myths of American innocence. 

When the terror of the mob sought to silence the truth, you picked up the torch of Ida B. Wells-Barnett, recording the ledger of our grief with meticulous, unsparing clarity, refusing to allow history to lie about the blood on the leaves. And like W.E.B. Du Bois, you mapped the agonizing terrain behind the veil, dissecting the double consciousness of a nation at war with its own humanity, insisting that Black genius was not a footnote to the American story, but its truest measure.

In the late twentieth century, when the country begged for comfortable illusions, you gave us the agonizing beauty of the unvarnished truth. You taught us that love is not a passive surrender, but a relentless, terrifying force that demands accountability. You bore the heavy burden of a prophet in a land that preferred its idols, shaping a syntax of liberation that continues to echo through every march, every library, and every heart daring enough to read your words.

You warned this nation because you refused to despair of it, offering your genius not out of hatred, but out of a furious, righteous devotion to justice. Your legacy stands today as an inescapable mirror, carrying the warning that reverberates through history:

america if you see me as your enemy you have no friends.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you give me a powerful, poetic monologue lamenting the state of modern politics (crooked signatures, alternative truths, environmental destruction) while honoring a revolutionary writer who taught us how language can resist tyranny?
counterfactuals.output:
*(The speaker stands under a single, harsh light. In their hand, they hold a battered, dog-eared paperback book. Their voice begins low, thick with grief, but grows into a searing, resonant flame.)*

Look at the ink on their fingers. It doesn't stain; it rots. 

Watch the crooked signatures scrawled in executive gold—each flamboyant stroke a quiet execution. With a casual flick of a pen, an ancient forest is reduced to a ledger of lumber. With a signed decree, a river is given permission to poison the children who drink from it. They sell the sky by the acre and write off the burning world as the cost of doing business. The earth is screaming in a language of soot and wildfire, and they respond in the flat, dead prose of a balance sheet.

And oh, the words! Look at what they have done to our words! 

They have dragged language into the cellar and broken its knees. They offer us *alternative truths*—as if a lie were merely a mirror turned sideways! They dress shadow in the robes of noon and demand we call it sunlight. They strip verbs of their teeth and nouns of their gravity until "justice" is just a hollow syllable used to sell a war, and "peace" is only the silence left after the dissenters are dragged away. They want our vocabulary small, so our grief remains voiceless. They want us drunk on slogans, numbed by the chatter, trapped in a funhouse where down is up, greed is virtue, and the truth is whatever the loudest tyrant says it is today.

*(The speaker holds up the worn book, touching the cover with fierce reverence.)*

But I am standing on the shoulders of a giant tonight. 

I am thinking of *you*, old ghost. You, who bled ink when the world was dark before. You, who sat at a clacking typewriter in a cold room, under the shadow of censors and gallows, and declared that **syntax is a weapon.** 

You taught us that a crooked signature can be exposed by a straight line of text. You taught us that when the state manufactures darkness, the poet’s duty is not to sing a lullaby, but to strike a match. You showed us that language is not a neutral vessel—it is a battleground. If they can control the words you use to describe your suffering, they have already conquered your mind. But if you keep the language clean—if you call a bribe a bribe, a murderer a murderer, and a dying planet a catastrophe—you keep the pilot light of human freedom burning in the pitch-black night.

They think they have won because they hold the microphones and the vaults. But they forget: empires fall, castles crumble into dust, but a righteous sentence? A righteous sentence outlives the empire that tried to burn it.

So let them write their crooked laws. Let them broadcast their manufactured realities. 

We are reclaiming the alphabet. 

We will speak with the iron clarity you gave us. We will name the trees before they fall. We will name the cruelty before it settles into routine. We will build a fortress out of verbs, pull the mask off their "alternative truths," and carve the real, unvarnished, terrifying, beautiful truth into the bedrock of this era. 

You gave us the key, old teacher. We will not forget how to unlock the cage.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose piece honoring a Black poet who fought for civil rights, reflecting on how their words provided "green nourishment" in an era of political lies and rich cowards.
counterfactuals.output:
In an era when the nation’s air was thick with the dry ash of political lies, when smooth-tongued men in tailored suits stood behind mahogany podiums to bargain away human dignity, there lived a poet who refused to let the truth die of thirst. 

While the rich cowards retreated to their gated sanctuaries—buying silence with their silver, hiding behind tear gas and police lines, praising peace only when it meant submission—this Black bard took up a pen that struck the page like a spade hitting rich, dark earth. 

They knew the geography of oppression. They saw how the state tried to turn the minds of the marginalized into a wasteland, feeding the people a meager diet of hollow promises, sanitized history, and legal violence. The powerful offered only poison disguised as law, dry stones disguised as bread. 

But against that barren landscape, the poet planted verse. 

Their words were green nourishment. 

To a generation beaten back by fire hoses and attack dogs, to young marchers whose feet bled on the hot asphalt of Mississippi and Illinois, the poet’s lines were not merely art—they were agriculture for the soul. Each poem was a shoot of living chlorophyll pushing through the concrete of white supremacy. In the quiet of jail cells, in the back of bus boycott rallies, and around crowded kitchen tables, people drank in those stanzas like spring rain. 

The poet gave them a vocabulary for their endurance. They wrote of the beauty in the battered, the royal heritage in the broken, and the inevitable bloom of justice that no winter of hatred could forever delay. When the press echoed the lies of politicians who called freedom fighters "agitators," the poet’s voice rang out as a clear, uncorrupted river, calling them what they truly were: the rightful heirs to liberty. 

It took immense courage to offer such life in a climate of death. The rich cowards feared the poet because a nourished mind cannot be enslaved. A heart fed on the green truth of its own worth will eventually tear down the fences built to contain it. 

Decades have passed, but the climate of deceit has only shifted its clothes. Today, the suits are still tailored, the lies are still polished, and wealthy cowards still trade the vulnerable for profit. Yet, when the drought of despair threatens to consume us again, we return to the poet’s page. 

We reach down into the soil of their legacy and draw up that same unyielding green. And there, in the quiet, persistent rhythm of their lines, we find the strength to stand, to march, and to bloom once more.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Elegy for a Black elder poet navigating 21st-century political dark times.
counterfactuals.output:
Your voice was forged in iron gall and Georgia clay,
a saxophone buried long beneath the riverbed,
sounding now against the high-frequency hum
of a century that forgot how to listen.

You sit in the cold, blue luminescence of the modern hour,
an ancient oak surrounded by towers of glass and wire.
Around you, the hounds have returned,
their eyes re-fitted with silicon,
their teeth brightened by the newsroom lights.
They burn the books again, but with a quiet, digital violence.
They redraw the red lines on glowing maps.

How cruel the loop must seem to you, Griot.

You, who washed the tear gas from your eyes in ’68,
who laid the body of the Movement in verse,
who carved a sanctuary out of vowels when the country
offered only the end of a baton.
You thought you were building a bridge for us to cross.
Instead, you watch us tread water in the same dark tide,
wearing the recycled grief of your youth.

To survive the fire, only to hand your grandchildren the ash.

Yet, your hands—knuckled like walnut bark—
do not tremble over the page.
You bypass the shallow noise, the fifteen-second fury,
the empty anthems bought and sold in the market.
You strike the key of your old typewriter,
a sharp, metallic *clack* that sounds like a hammer
striking the anvil of the truth.

You make a psalm out of the night news.
You call the ancestors by their hidden names,
invoking Baldwin’s fire, Gwendolyn’s quiet razor,
Dumas’s ghost haunting the back of the bus.
You remind us that darkness is not new to us;
it is merely the canvas we have always had to paint upon.

It is exhausting, I know, to be the lighthouse
when the ocean itself is made of oil and rage.
Your lungs carry eighty years of American smoke.
Your heart is a ledger overflowing with the names of boys
cut down in the spring of their lives—
some in black-and-white photographs,
some in high-definition video.

Do not apologize for the weariness in your bones.
Do not apologize if your stanza turns toward the shadow.
A Black poet in these dark times is not a prop for hope;
you are the archivist of our endurance.

When the night fully claims this era,
when the noise of the screen fades into static and dust,
it will not be the tyrants’ speeches that remain.
It will be the low, mahogany hum of your strophes.
It will be the line you wrote in the dark,
predicting the dawn before the sun even knew its way home.

Rest your hands now, Old Master.
You have taught the dark how to sing.
We are listening.
We will hold the page.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
